title: Bellman-Ford & negative cycles
overview: Bellman-Ford finds single-source shortest paths even with negative edge weights. It simply relaxes every edge n−1 times. One more round that still improves a distance proves a negative cycle, where no shortest path exists.

concepts.explain: Bellman-Ford loops over all edges, so an edge list (`a`, `b`, `c`) is the natural storage; here each edge is an `Edge` object.
A shortest path uses at most n−1 edges, so n−1 full rounds are enough to settle every distance.
Skip edges whose start is still infinite; otherwise `INT_MAX + c` overflows.
Run one extra round. If any edge still relaxes, a cycle with negative total weight is reachable.
O(V·E): slower than Dijkstra, but it handles negative edges.

check_yourself.q: Bellman-Ford vs Dijkstra: which is faster, and which handles negative weights?
check_yourself.a: Dijkstra is faster (O((V+E) log V)); Bellman-Ford handles negative weights (O(V·E)).

check_yourself.q: For an undirected graph with a negative edge, what does Bellman-Ford report?
check_yourself.a: A negative cycle, because the edge can be walked back and forth.
Yes: if a full round changes nothing, all distances are final.

body: Module 7 ended with a warning: Dijkstra is not allowed when an edge can be negative. This module is the answer to exactly that case.

Negative weights are not a made-up puzzle. Think of a journey where one leg pays you back more than it costs - a refund, a discount, a currency trade that gains. The cost of that leg is a negative number, and the cheapest overall route may well go through it.

Why does Dijkstra fall over? Because it rests on one promise: the moment a node is the nearest unfinished one, its distance is final and it is never looked at again. With every weight zero or more that promise is safe. Add one negative edge and a node you already declared finished can become cheaper afterwards, and the algorithm never goes back to notice.

Bellman-Ford throws that cleverness away. It does not choose a clever order at all. It just **relaxes every edge in the graph, over and over**. Because it never declares anything final, nothing can catch it out.

How many rounds are enough? A shortest route never repeats a node, so with n nodes it uses at most n-1 edges. One full round over all the edges settles at least one more edge of that route, whatever order the edges happen to be in. So **n-1 rounds is always enough** - no more is needed, and no fewer is safe.
Take four nodes and four directed edges, stored as a plain edge list, and start from node 0. Note the edge `2 -> 1` costs -3:
Here is round one, one edge at a time. A dash means "still unknown":

Watch node 1. The direct edge put a 4 there, and then the negative edge from node 2 rewrote it: 5 - 3 = 2, so the two-edge route wins. Dijkstra, having already finished node 1 at 4, would never have looked again.
Round two changes nothing, and so does round three; the table is settled. Each round is the same four lines of code:
That `dis[ed.a] != INT_MAX` guard matters: without it you would add a weight to `INT_MAX`, overflow the `int`, and get a huge negative number that looks like a wonderful route.
Now the second half of the module. Three nodes, with `1 -> 2` costing -4 and `2 -> 1` costing 1, so one lap of that little loop gains you -3 every time:
intro.trace:
edges: 0->1 (2)   1->2 (-4)   2->1 (1)

             0    1    2
start        0    -    -
round 1      0   -1   -2
round 2      0   -4   -5
extra round  0   -7   -8   still falling

body: With n = 3 you do n-1 = 2 rounds and stop. But run **one extra round** and the distances drop again, by 3, and they would drop by 3 more every round for ever. There is no shortest route here: go round the loop once more and you always beat your own answer. That is a negative cycle, and the extra round is how you detect it - if any edge still relaxes after n-1 rounds, say so and stop.

The price is O(V.E): for 1000 nodes and 5000 edges that is about 5 million relaxations, clearly slower than Dijkstra's O((V + E) log V). So the rule for choosing is short. All weights zero or more: Dijkstra, and it is faster. Any weight negative: Bellman-Ford, and you get a negative-cycle test for one extra round of work.

The programs below write it twice - plain, then with the cycle check - and once more in the shape a judge wants, where the distances start at 10^8 instead of `INT_MAX` and a negative cycle is reported as `{-1}`. Read the watch-out notes as you go: two of the three files have small mistakes worth spotting yourself.

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: one edge relaxed at a time
body: The four directed edges of `bellman-ford.cpp`, always tried in the same order, starting from node 0. A dash means still unknown. Watch node 1: the direct edge gives it a 4, and then the negative edge takes it back off again.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows to relax the edges

frames.label: Only the source has a number. Every other node is unknown, which the real program stores as `INT_MAX`.
Round 1, edge 0->1 costing 4. Node 0 is known, and 0 + 4 is better than unknown, so `dis[1] = 4`.
Round 1, edge 2->1 costing -3. This is the moment. 5 - 3 = 2, which is less than the 4 already written, so node 1 is rewritten. The longer route wins because one of its edges pays you back.
Round 1, edge 1->3 costing 2. It uses the brand-new 2, so `dis[3] = 4`. Round one is over and the table reads 0, 2, 5, 4.
Round 2 starts again from the top. Edge 2->1 is re-checked: 5 - 3 = 2, which is not less than the 2 already there, so nothing moves. Bellman-Ford never knows it is finished; it just keeps asking.
frames.art:
0 --4--> 1 --2--> 3
  |        ^
  5        |
  |       -3
  v        |
  2 -------+

edge order: 0->1  0->2  2->1  1->3

node     0    1    2    3
dis      0    2    5    4
     no change anywhere in round 2

frames.label: Round 3 - with n = 4 nodes you do n-1 = 3 rounds - changes nothing either. That is the guarantee: a shortest route uses at most 3 edges, and each round settles at least one more of them.
frames.art:
0 --4--> 1 --2--> 3
  |        ^
  5        |
  |       -3
  v        |
  2 -------+

edge order: 0->1  0->2  2->1  1->3

node     0    1    2    3
dis      0    2    5    4
     no change anywhere in round 3

frames.label: The final distances from node 0. Dijkstra would have declared node 1 finished at 4 the moment it was nearest, and never looked again - so it would have printed 4 here, and 6 for node 3. Blind repetition is what saves Bellman-Ford.

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: a table that never settles
body: Three nodes now, from `bellman_ford_cycle.cpp`. Going 1 -> 2 costs -4 and coming back 2 -> 1 costs 1, so one lap of that little loop gains you -3. Watch the two numbers on the right: they never stop falling.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows to run the rounds

frames.label: Start at node 0, nothing else known.
Round 1, edge 1->2 costing -4: 2 - 4 = -2, so `dis[2] = -2`. Negative distances are perfectly legal here.
Round 1, edge 2->1 costing 1: -2 + 1 = -1, which beats the 2, so node 1 drops. Round one ends at 0, -1, -2.
Round 2 runs the same three edges. 0->1 changes nothing, but 1->2 gives -5 and then 2->1 gives -4. Both numbers have fallen by exactly 3 again.
With n = 3 nodes the algorithm does n-1 = 2 rounds and stops. So this row is what it would print: 0, -4, -5. It looks like a perfectly ordinary answer.
frames.art:
0 --2--> 1 --(-4)--> 2
           ^           |
           +-----1-----+

edge order: 0->1 (2)  1->2 (-4)  2->1 (1)

node      0     1     2
dis       0    -4    -5
      this is what the program would print

frames.label: Now run one extra round, the one the code does only as a test. The numbers fall by 3 yet again. An edge that still relaxes after n-1 rounds means something is wrong.

And it would fall by 3 every round for ever, because you can go round the loop again and always beat your own answer. There is no shortest route to node 1 at all, so the honest output is not a number - it is "negative cycle".
frames.art:
0 --2--> 1 --(-4)--> 2
           ^           |
           +-----1-----+

edge order: 0->1 (2)  1->2 (-4)  2->1 (1)

node      0     1     2
dis       0   ...   ...
      no shortest route exists: report it
